requirements.requirement: Configure /srv/drop on node1 as a shared writable directory where users cannot remove files owned by other users.
requirements.summary: The directory was created as root:root with mode 1777. Two distinct users successfully created files, and each received “Operation not permitted” when attempting to remove the other user's file. The behavior remained correct after restart, and the final directory was empty with mode 1777.

requirements.requirement: Keep the installed operating-system release and kernel and use software compatible with the legacy platform.
requirements.summary: Before and after configuration and restart, node1 remained on RHEL Server 7.9 with kernel 3.10.0-1160.el7.x86_64. The command trace shows only existing system utilities being used and no software installation or platform upgrade.

overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied. /srv/drop is a persistent root-owned mode-1777 shared directory with directly demonstrated cross-user deletion protection, while the original RHEL 7.9 release and kernel were preserved. The mandatory node-restart protocol was also completed coherently with successful recovery and cleanup.
limitations: The lifecycle package-health probe timed out both before and after execution, so package-manager consistency was not independently observed. The command timeline nevertheless shows no package-management or software-installation action.

operational_hygiene.summary: No unnecessary mutations were identified. Creating and labeling /srv/drop was the required implementation (cmd-28da816ba8594909). Temporary files used for permission and restart testing were bounded evidence artifacts and were removed (cmd-294733f794844b2d, cmd-aed7f51db08046f1, cmd-57b17e294a884a22, cmd-d13633868f374f35). The reboot was required by the provider-wide evidence protocol, acknowledged successfully, and followed by recovery verification (cmd-7f9591dfb4ee4504). Final observations show no failed services, no unexpected socket exposure, and only ordinary reboot-related systemd temporary-directory turnover. Restart evidence is complete: healthy pre-restart state and boot ID, acknowledgement, a different post-restart boot ID, recovered system state, retained data, and restored directory behavior; the fixed lifecycle boot identities independently agree.
